questions.question: Describe how world population has grown over time, explain what caused the population explosion, and explain why the population still rises even though the growth rate has been falling since the late 1960s.
questions.expected_answer: For nearly all of human history population grew extremely slowly, because high birth rates were cancelled by almost equally high death rates from famine, disease and infant death; the world only reached one billion around 1804. Then the curve exploded: two billion by 1927, three billion by 1960, and roughly a new billion every twelve years after that — four billion in 1974, five in 1987, six in 1999, seven in 2011 and eight in 2022 — forming a J-curve, flat for centuries and then almost vertical. The explosion was caused not by rising births but by collapsing deaths: the agricultural and industrial revolutions increased food, and clean water, sewerage, vaccination and antibiotics cut death rates, while birth rates stayed high for generations, widening natural increase. Growth was fastest after 1950 when medicine reached Asia, Africa and Latin America within a single generation. The growth rate peaked at about two per cent in the late 1960s and has fallen below one per cent, yet population still rises because a falling positive rate still means growth, and because of population momentum: the huge cohorts born in high-fertility decades are now parents, so even small families produce many total births. Projections show the curve levelling out above ten billion late this century — the J-curve becoming an S-curve.

questions.question: Define overpopulation and carrying capacity, use the Netherlands and the Sahel to show why overpopulation is not the same as high density, and list the signs by which an overpopulated region can be recognised.
questions.expected_answer: A region is overpopulated when its population exceeds its carrying capacity — the number of people the area's resources and technology can support at a decent standard of living. Overpopulation is a ratio between people and resources, not a headcount or a density figure. The Netherlands, with more than 500 people per square kilometre, is one of the densest countries on earth yet not overpopulated, because fertile land, advanced technology and a strong economy support its people at a high standard of living. Parts of the arid Sahel, with fewer than 20 people per square kilometre, can be overpopulated because rainfall is so scarce and soils so thin that even that sparse population presses beyond what the land can regenerate. The signs of overpopulation are the symptoms of strain: land pressure with plots subdivided smaller each generation and farming pushed onto marginal ground; environmental degradation through overgrazing, deforestation for fuelwood, soil erosion and falling water tables; unemployment as the workforce outgrows jobs; overcrowded schools and clinics, housing shortages and informal settlements outpacing services; and ultimately hunger and outmigration of the young. Carrying capacity is not fixed: irrigation, fertiliser and improved seed raise it, while erosion, exhausted groundwater and drought lower it, so a region can become overpopulated without any population growth at all.

questions.question: Discuss the strategies for managing population growth, contrasting China's one-child policy with the voluntary approach of Kerala and Thailand, and show where South Africa fits.
questions.expected_answer: The most effective strategies change the conditions under which families make choices. The strongest is the education of girls and women: educated women marry later, have wider choices, earn incomes that make each child's schooling worth investing in, and use family planning effectively — no policy has cut birth rates as reliably. Second, reducing infant mortality: parents in high-mortality regions have extra children as insurance against losing some, so when clinics, vaccination and clean water make survival normal, families shrink within a generation. Third, accessible and affordable family planning with honest information. Fourth, poverty reduction and social security, especially pensions, which remove children's role as a retirement plan. China's one-child policy, enforced with fines from 1979 to 2015, cut births but left an ageing population arriving before the country grew rich, a shrinking workforce and a skewed sex ratio with millions more boys than girls; birth rates now barely respond to encouragement to grow. Thailand and Kerala achieved comparable fertility declines through education, healthcare and voluntary family planning, without coercion or demographic scars — showing choice outperforms force. South Africa followed the voluntary route: fertility fell from about six children per woman in the 1960s to about 2,3 today through urbanisation, women's education, clinic-based family planning and falling infant mortality, leaving growth near one per cent and easing.
